title: Slowest Pace That Beats the Deadline
statement:
A translator has a book split into chapters; chapter i has pages[i] pages. She works at a fixed pace of speed pages per hour, and she has hours hours before the deadline.

Each hour she works on one chapter only. She translates up to speed pages of it; if the chapter has fewer pages left, she finishes it and idles for the rest of that hour instead of starting another chapter.

Return the smallest whole number speed that lets her finish every chapter within hours hours. It is guaranteed that hours ≥ pages.length, so an answer always exists.

examples.why: At 4 pages an hour the chapters take 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 hours. At 3 they take 2 + 4 + 2 = 8, which is too many.
18 pages over 3 hours averages 6, but at speed 6 each chapter takes 2 hours, 4 in total. Hours cannot be shared between chapters, so one chapter must fit in a single hour: speed 9.
One hour per chapter, so the pace must cover the longest chapter in one go.

hints: Forget the minimum for a moment. If someone hands you a speed, can you check whether it is fast enough?
If speed 40 is fast enough, is 41? If 39 is too slow, is 38? Picture the answer to 'fast enough?' for every speed from 1 upward.
That picture is no, no, …, no, yes, yes, … . Binary search for the first yes between 1 and the longest chapter. Checking one speed costs O(n): add up ceil(pages[i] / speed).

explain.intuition:
Nothing here is sorted, so where is the binary search? It runs over the answer, not over the input. Ask a yes/no question about a candidate speed: "can she finish in time at this pace?" A faster pace never takes longer, so the answers line up as no no no … yes yes yes. The smallest speed that works is where the first yes appears, and binary search finds that edge with about 30 checks even when speeds go up to 10⁹.

This is "binary search on the answer", and it shows up whenever you need the smallest (or largest) value that passes a test, and passing is monotone. Think of finding the narrowest breakpoint where a layout stops wrapping: you would not try every pixel width. The range is 1 … max(pages): no answer is below 1, and at max(pages) every chapter takes exactly one hour, which always fits because hours ≥ pages.length.
steps: Write fits(speed): add up ceil(pages[i] / speed) and compare with hours. Stop early once the total is over.
Set lo = 1, hi = max(pages). Promise: the answer is always in [lo, hi], and hi always fits.
While lo < hi, take mid = lo + floor((hi − lo) / 2), which rounds down.
If fits(mid), then mid might be the answer: hi = mid. Otherwise everything up to mid is too slow: lo = mid + 1.
The loop stops when lo === hi; that single value is the answer.
pitfalls: Writing hi = mid − 1 when mid fits. If mid was the smallest speed that works, you just threw the answer away.

Rounding mid up while using hi = mid / lo = mid + 1. With lo = 3, hi = 4 the rounded-up mid is 4; if it fits, hi stays 4 and the loop never ends. Round down when the shrinking step is hi = mid, round up when it is lo = mid.

Starting at the average ceil(sum / hours) and returning it, or computing mid with (lo + hi) >> 1. The first ignores that hours cannot be shared (second example). The second is a trap waiting for bigger limits: JavaScript's >> works on 32-bit integers. Here lo + hi stays just under 2³¹, but with pages up to 2·10⁹ the sum would wrap to a negative number without any error.

complexity.time: O(n log M), where M = max(pages)

solutions.title: Try every speed from 1 upward
solutions.idea: Return the first speed that fits. Correct, but with chapters of 10⁹ pages it can try a billion speeds.

solutions.title: Binary search on the speed
solutions.idea: Whether a speed fits is monotone: once it fits, every faster speed fits too. Search 1 … max(pages) for the first speed that fits.

followups: She may now split an hour between chapters. What is the answer then, and do you still need a search?

Chapters must be done in order and you have k translators, each taking a contiguous run of chapters. Minimise the largest number of pages any one of them gets. Why does the same search-on-the-answer idea work?
